name: Lazurite
toxicityNote: Sulfur-bearing and sensitive to acids; avoid soaking and do not make elixirs.
physical: Traditionally linked to calm and relaxation
Associated with easing tension in the head
Kept nearby by many for peaceful, focused evenings
summary: Lazurite is the intense blue mineral that gives lapis lazuli its color, and crystal lore links it to wisdom, truth and deep intuition.
intro: Lazurite is the mineral that makes lapis lazuli blue. On its own it forms rare, deep blue crystals, usually dense and granular, with a velvety look when raw and a rich glow when polished. The color is an intense ultramarine to violet-blue, sometimes with white calcite veining or flecks of golden pyrite. Pure lazurite is harder to find than lapis, which is a rock containing lazurite along with calcite and pyrite, and specimens usually come from the same famous source: the Sar-i-Sang mines of Badakhshan in Afghanistan. It is a stone with a long and distinguished history, and a quiet power that is hard to ignore.
history: Lazurite takes its name from the Persian lazhward, meaning blue or heaven, the same root that gave us azure and lapis lazuli. The Sar-i-Sang mines in Afghanistan have supplied lapis for over six thousand years, and lazurite-bearing stone has been found in ancient Egyptian jewelry, including the burial mask of Tutankhamun, and in Mesopotamian artifacts. Renaissance painters ground it into ultramarine pigment, which cost more than gold, and used it for the robes of the Virgin Mary. The mineral name was formalized in 1890, but the stone's fame is far older, and it has been associated with royalty, wisdom and the heavens throughout history.
meaning: Lazurite is regarded as a stone of truth and inner vision. Because it is the heart of lapis, it carries the same associations with wisdom, royalty and honest expression, but practitioners say its energy is more concentrated. It is linked to the third eye and throat, and used for meditation, intuition and speaking one's truth with grace. Many use it when they need to cut through illusion and see a situation clearly. Its deep blue is also associated with calm, depth and dignity. Traditionally it is thought to promote a peaceful, composed mood and a relaxed head, and it is often kept near the workspace or altar.
howToUse: Keep a lazurite piece or lapis specimen with visible blue on your desk or altar as a reminder to speak and act truthfully. Rest it on your brow during meditation while lying down, and breathe slowly as you picture a deep blue night sky. Wear a small cabochon pendant at the throat when you have to say something difficult. In journaling rituals, hold it while you write unfiltered thoughts, then review what you wrote. Combine it with sodalite and blue lace agate for a calm, clear communication grid.
care: Lazurite is moderately hard but reacts with acids and can lose its polish in water over time, so keep it dry. Wipe with a soft dry cloth and avoid household cleaners, vinegar and ultrasonic cleaners. Cleanse with sound, smoke, moonlight or a bed of selenite. Sunlight in moderation is safe, though extremes of heat should be avoided. Store it wrapped in a cloth, away from harder stones that could scratch it.
identify: Genuine lazurite is a deep, saturated blue with a velvety surface and sometimes white calcite or golden pyrite flecks. Sodalite is similar but more blue-grey with white veining and no pyrite, while dyed howlite and dyed jasper show uneven, too-bright color that rubs off with acetone. Glass imitations show bubbles and a uniform look. Most gem material is natural, though some lapis is dyed or waxed to deepen color.

faq.q: What is the difference between lazurite and lapis lazuli?
faq.a: Lazurite is the blue mineral itself, while lapis lazuli is a rock made mostly of lazurite along with white calcite and golden pyrite. Pure lazurite is rarer, so most blue stones sold are lapis.

Practitioners use lazurite for wisdom, honest expression and intuitive vision. Its deep blue color is linked to the third eye and throat, and it is often held during meditation or before difficult conversations.
Avoid it. Lazurite contains sulfur and reacts with acids, so water soaks can dull the finish. Wipe with a dry soft cloth and cleanse with sound, smoke or moonlight instead of immersion.
